newsitem.title: GERMANY: Mercedes workers stay at home in protest.
newsitem.headline: Mercedes workers stay at home in protest.

text.p: Mercedes workers at three major factories stayed away from work on Saturday in protest at the company's decision to cut sick pay from October 1, the engineering union IG Metall said.

Only a few hundred of a total staff of 20,000 at the plants in Sindelfingen, Untertuerkheim and Bremen turned up for work after the works council suspended an agreement to work extra Saturday shifts to cope with high demand.
The stay-away prevented the production of 1,100 cars and 1,300 engines, after workers had already disrupted production of around 1,000 Mercedes cars in Bremen on Thursday.
The union plans another day of protests next Tuesday.

Mercedes's parent Daimler-Benz AG was the first big German industrial group to announce that it would enforce a 20 percent cut in sick pay from October 1 for its 220,000 workers. Several big companies, including Siemens AG, have followed suit.
Daimler chief executive Juergen Schrempp defended the move, saying that the cuts in labour-related costs were needed to help defend German jobs and production.
"I call this credible, resolute action. We are fighting for Germany as a place to do business, for jobs and thus for its workers," Schrempp told the Focus news magazine.

Schrempp dismissed calls for a general strike and said that unions should return to the negotiating table. "Nothing was ever resolved in the streets," he said in an interview to be published in the Monday edition of Focus.

Leaders of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's conservative coalition have criticised company bosses for rushing to implement the sick pay cuts. The measures were passed two weeks ago as part of a major austerity plan designed to stimulate job creation in Germany, where unemployment is close to post-war highs.
Union leaders and some politicians argue the legislation cannot be used to override existing pay agreements where full pay is stipulated.
